questions.domain: Governance, Standards, Policy and Sustainability Reporting
questions.prompt: Leadership asks for a “carbon-neutral digital platform” label based mainly on offsets. How do you respond?
questions.preferred_answer: Request the full life-cycle inventory, reduction trajectory, boundary, market-based claims, residual emissions and offset quality. Recommend reporting measured footprint and reductions separately from neutralisation claims, with independent review and precise wording. A label should not hide continuing growth or supply-chain impact.

questions.domain: GreenOps, FinOps and Business Value
questions.prompt: What is GreenOps, and how does it relate to FinOps?
questions.preferred_answer: GreenOps applies operational ownership, measurement and optimisation to environmental impact. FinOps aligns cloud value, cost and accountability. They overlap through utilisation, rightsizing, forecasting and workload decisions, but carbon, water and embodied impact do not always follow price, so sustainability requires additional signals and limits.

questions.domain: GreenOps, FinOps and Business Value
questions.prompt: Why can cost savings be a useful but incomplete sustainability proxy?
questions.preferred_answer: Reduced resource use often lowers both cost and impact, making cost a practical starting signal. Pricing also reflects margins, discounts, scarcity and commercial strategy rather than physical energy or emissions. Validate material decisions with resource and environmental data, especially across regions and service types.

questions.domain: GreenOps, FinOps and Business Value
questions.prompt: How should cloud sustainability responsibility be distributed?
questions.preferred_answer: Executives set goals and constraints; finance and sustainability define accounting; platform teams provide data and efficient defaults; service owners manage demand and architecture; procurement manages suppliers; and engineers act on workloads. A central team should enable and assure, not own every resource decision.

questions.domain: GreenOps, FinOps and Business Value
questions.prompt: How would you prioritise a portfolio of GreenOps opportunities?
questions.preferred_answer: Rank by credible absolute reduction, implementation effort, service risk, cost, data confidence, repeatability and strategic value. Start with waste removal and high-impact defaults, then architecture changes. Avoid selecting only projects with attractive percentages but negligible total effect.

questions.domain: GreenOps, FinOps and Business Value
questions.prompt: How can sustainability be connected to product and customer value?
questions.preferred_answer: Link actions to reliability, speed, affordability, hardware reach, regulatory readiness, supply resilience and user trust, while reporting environmental outcomes directly. Do not force every action into immediate revenue. Some value is avoided risk, resource security or the ability to operate within future constraints.

questions.domain: GreenOps, FinOps and Business Value
questions.prompt: What problems arise when teams are charged only for cloud cost but not environmental impact?
questions.preferred_answer: They may choose cheaper high-carbon regions, ignore embodied or water effects, retain discounted waste or optimise commitments rather than resource use. Add environmental signals, shared guardrails and service-level budgets while avoiding false precision. Incentives should reward verified outcomes, not dashboard movement.

questions.domain: GreenOps, FinOps and Business Value
questions.prompt: Could internal carbon pricing improve IT decisions?
questions.preferred_answer: A shadow or internal fee can make emissions visible in investment choices and fund reduction, but it depends on credible boundaries and a price high enough to affect behaviour. It must not become permission to emit or replace physical budgets. Pair it with absolute targets, technical standards and transparent exceptions.

questions.domain: GreenOps, FinOps and Business Value
questions.prompt: An optimisation saves £500,000 annually but increases emissions because workloads move to a dirtier region. What should happen?
questions.preferred_answer: Quantify the emissions, service constraints and alternatives; make the trade-off visible to authorised owners; and test efficiency, contractual and scheduling options. Apply the organisation’s carbon target or internal price, but do not hide the outcome in cost success. The final decision should state who benefits and who bears the environmental cost.

questions.domain: Organisational Change, Ethics and Rebound Effects
questions.prompt: Why do sustainability programmes fail when treated only as technical optimisation?
questions.preferred_answer: Technology choices are shaped by incentives, product goals, budgets, procurement, skills and power. Engineers may remove waste while the business creates more demand. Successful change aligns leadership objectives, team ownership, data, decision rights and product strategy, and makes trade-offs discussable.

questions.domain: Organisational Change, Ethics and Rebound Effects
questions.prompt: What does climate justice add to Green IT decision-making?
questions.preferred_answer: It asks who benefits from digital services and who bears extraction, energy, water, pollution, labour and e-waste burdens. Decisions should consider vulnerable communities, workers and future generations, include participation and avoid shifting impact across borders. Efficiency alone does not answer fairness.

questions.domain: Organisational Change, Ethics and Rebound Effects
questions.prompt: How can sustainability become part of normal engineering work?
questions.preferred_answer: Add it to requirements, architecture reviews, platform defaults, incident and capacity processes, procurement, dashboards and retrospectives. Train teams using role-relevant examples and give them actionable data. Avoid a separate volunteer programme that disappears under delivery pressure.

questions.domain: Organisational Change, Ethics and Rebound Effects
questions.prompt: Why can employee-awareness campaigns have limited impact?
questions.preferred_answer: Individual actions matter, but most IT impact is locked into architecture, procurement, product demand and supplier choices. Campaigns without structural options can shift responsibility to employees. Pair awareness with policies, budgets, approved alternatives and leadership decisions that change the system.

questions.domain: Organisational Change, Ethics and Rebound Effects
questions.prompt: How should conflicts between sustainability, accessibility, privacy, cost and speed be resolved?
questions.preferred_answer: Identify non-negotiable legal, safety and rights requirements, quantify remaining trade-offs, include affected stakeholders, compare alternatives and assign an authorised owner. Document assumptions and review outcomes. Do not optimise one metric by exporting harm to people who lack decision power.

questions.domain: Organisational Change, Ethics and Rebound Effects
questions.prompt: How can organisations detect rebound after an efficiency programme?
questions.preferred_answer: Track absolute demand, service volume, unit cost, feature growth, user behaviour and infrastructure expansion before and after the change. Separate planned growth from efficiency-induced growth where possible through experiments or counterfactual analysis. Respond with product, pricing, quota or policy changes, not only another efficiency round.

questions.domain: Organisational Change, Ethics and Rebound Effects
questions.prompt: What would a sufficiency review ask before approving an IT initiative?
questions.preferred_answer: It asks whether the need is legitimate, whether an existing service can meet it, the minimum quality and scale, who benefits, what demand it may induce and what environmental budget it consumes. It compares smaller, slower, shared, repaired and no-build options. Approval should depend on value within limits, not novelty.

questions.domain: Organisational Change, Ethics and Rebound Effects
questions.prompt: A sustainability team is praised for lowering emissions per employee while the company’s total digital footprint doubles. How should success be evaluated?
questions.preferred_answer: Acknowledge operational efficiency but assess absolute life-cycle impact, business growth, acquisitions, cloud and supplier boundaries and whether targets align with climate limits. Intensity can be informative, but it cannot substitute for total reduction. Reframe incentives so the team can challenge demand and strategy, not just optimise ratios.

questions.domain: Future of Green Computing and Critical Reflection
questions.prompt: What is an IT carbon budget, and how is it different from a reduction target?
questions.preferred_answer: A carbon budget sets a cumulative or periodic emissions limit within which digital services must operate. A reduction target specifies a change from a baseline by a date. Budgets force prioritisation among competing workloads and expose growth assumptions; they need clear boundaries, allocation, uncertainty and exception governance.

questions.domain: Future of Green Computing and Critical Reflection
questions.prompt: How could electricity availability become an application architecture constraint?
questions.preferred_answer: Grid connection delays, local capacity and hourly supply may limit when and where compute can grow. Applications may need queueing, flexible service levels, efficient models, local energy awareness and resource budgets. Architecture would treat power as a constrained dependency like latency or memory, not an unlimited utility.

questions.domain: Future of Green Computing and Critical Reflection
questions.prompt: When is “do not compute” the technically superior answer?
questions.preferred_answer: When computation adds little value, duplicates existing results, is used mainly to manipulate attention, or consumes disproportionate resources and risk. A technically mature team can remove demand, simplify a feature or choose a deterministic process. Optimisation should follow a justified need, not protect every idea from scrutiny.

questions.domain: Future of Green Computing and Critical Reflection
questions.prompt: What governance is required for autonomous carbon-aware infrastructure?
questions.preferred_answer: Define authorised objectives and hard constraints, validated data sources, uncertainty thresholds, safe fallback, audit logs, human override, fairness review and responsibility for failures. Test interactions with markets, grids and service-level controls. The system should optimise verified net outcomes, not chase a single fluctuating signal.

questions.domain: Future of Green Computing and Critical Reflection
questions.prompt: How might digital product passports and data-centre minimum standards reshape IT roles?
questions.preferred_answer: Professionals may need to manage machine-readable lifecycle data, verify repair and material claims, connect product records to asset systems, and design workloads for rated facilities. New work will span engineering, procurement, audit and policy. Skills in data assurance and lifecycle reasoning will matter alongside technical optimisation.

questions.domain: Future of Green Computing and Critical Reflection
questions.prompt: Which skills will distinguish future Sustainable IT professionals?
questions.preferred_answer: Systems thinking, carbon and energy accounting, software and cloud architecture, data-centre fundamentals, LCA, procurement, circularity, measurement uncertainty, policy interpretation, stakeholder facilitation and ethical judgement. The role requires challenging demand and translating evidence into decisions, not merely operating a carbon dashboard.

questions.domain: Future of Green Computing and Critical Reflection
questions.prompt: Can Green IT unintentionally legitimise unlimited digital expansion?
questions.preferred_answer: Yes. Efficiency labels and renewable claims can reduce scrutiny of total demand, hardware growth, water, extraction and attention economy effects. Green IT is credible only when it reports absolute life-cycle impact, addresses rebound and allows the conclusion that some growth or features should not proceed.

resolution.title: Key Questions on Energy and AI

questions.domain: Future of Green Computing and Critical Reflection
questions.prompt: By 2030, the board wants twice the AI output with no increase in life-cycle emissions. How would you test whether this is feasible and responsible?
questions.preferred_answer: Define valuable output and the full boundary; establish current training, inference, hardware, data-centre, water and supply-chain impact; model efficiency, grid and hardware scenarios; and test rebound. Set quality and social-value thresholds, absolute budgets and stop conditions. If credible pathways do not fit the budget, reduce demand or reject the growth target rather than rely on speculative future efficiency.

evaluation_rubric.interpretation: No usable answer, unsafe recommendation, greenwashing claim or serious misconception.
Recognises part of the topic but misses the environmental mechanism, system boundary or practical control.
Accurate concept and one relevant action, with limited measurement, uncertainty or trade-off depth.
Applies the concept to implementation, evidence, lifecycle effects, failure modes and realistic trade-offs.
Production-grade judgement: prioritises safely, challenges unnecessary demand, explains alternatives and protects social as well as environmental outcomes.

publishing_guidance: Hide preferred answers until an attempt is submitted or the learner selects View resolution.
Score concepts and judgement against evaluation points rather than exact wording.
Display source owner, source tier and last-verified date beside every resolution link.
Allow filters for role, domain, difficulty, question type, future focus, critical reflection and practical-versus-theory.
Require both absolute and intensity metrics where demand growth can alter the conclusion.
Do not imply that a score, badge, offset or efficiency improvement guarantees lower total environmental impact or an employer-assessment result.
